I'm a 44-year-old woman farming 2.6 mu in Quzhou. I've been doing this for 20 years, and my family has seven mouths to feed, though some of the younger ones work off-farm and send a bit home. I only finished primary school, so I don't read those extension leaflets much — I watch what my neighbors do and I remember what happened on my own fields.

**This year, here's how I'm thinking:**

The maize just came off the field — or it will in the next few days — and I need to get the wheat in by mid-October. The turnaround is always tight. My neighbor Wang across the lane tried saving money on seed two years ago and bought some cheap stuff from the open market. His wheat was thin and patchy, and he ended up losing more than he saved. I remember that, so I still buy my seed from the county supply store, but I only buy exactly what I need for 2.6 mu.

For fertilizer, I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting — about 25 kg — and work it into the soil. Last year the wheat looked a bit yellow at jointing because the spring was dry, so I topdressed with urea. I plan to do the same this year: if the wheat looks off at jointing, I'll put another 15 kg of urea per mu. It costs more, but if I skip it and the weather turns bad, I'll lose a lot more. I'd rather waste a little fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. I can't afford those big losses.

I irrigate wheat three times: once before winter to help it settle, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if it's dry. My well is metered and pumping isn't free, but wheat is my main cash crop for the year, so I give it the water. For the summer maize, the rains usually come in July and August, so I only plan two irrigations — one right after planting if it's dry, and one during tasseling if the rain doesn't show up.

For corn, everything has to go fast. Between wheat harvest and corn planting, sometimes I only have two or three days. I do one quick pass with the rotary tiller, or sometimes no-till if the ground is soft, then plant immediately. All the fertilizer for corn goes in at planting — compound fertilizer in the furrow — because there's no time to come back and topdress later. The corn season is too short.

I don't hire labor. On 2.6 mu, paying 150 yuan per day for a worker would eat my whole margin. My family does everything — planting, harvesting, carrying bags. My son sends money from the city, but I don't want to ask him for farm money. This is my responsibility, and I manage with what I have.
